scope: Paris-London art criticism, 1699-1813 (critics active 1708-1765), three critics with documented but different routes to standing
note: v0.2. The De Piles and Richardson reception rows are sourced from texts read in full-text scans (editions and pages in each 'source'; scans listed in docs/sources.md). Level rule used for every row: a single named receiver or editor acting alone is 'coterie'; a body acting formally is 'field'; 'canon' needs a source that says so and none was found. Confidence: high = primary text read; medium = authoritative secondary read, or a primary read with an estimated date; low = unsourced. Unsourced rows are kept as low and cannot carry the verdict. Nothing here is a finding about whether any critic was right.

French-reading public on the Continent (via the Amsterdam translation)

later scholars, editors, markets and canon-makers

critics.name: Roger de Piles
critics.position: amateur: Conseiller honoraire of the Academie royale from 1699 (Procès-verbaux III p. 259; listed 'Conseiller-Amateur' IV p. 81 by inference), outside its teaching hierarchy

claims.text: painting and sculpture need certain principles, which an amateur can state to the Academie (Discours read 6 July 1699)
painters can be compared on numbered scales (composition, drawing, colour, expression); offered 'plutot pour me divertir que pour attirer les autres dans mon sentiment'

critics.name: Jonathan Richardson
critics.position: London portrait painter and theorist addressing gentlemen who are 'Lovers' and 'Connoisseurs' or may become so (Two Discourses 1719, discourse II p. 157)

claims.text: connoisseurship is a science with dignity, certainty, pleasure and advantage, open to gentlemen (title of Two Discourses, discourse II)

critics.name: Denis Diderot
critics.position: man of letters writing outside any art institution

claims.text: the Salon review is itself a literary work whose standing is the writer's own

events.source: Montaiglon (ed.), Proces-verbaux de l'Academie royale de peinture et de sculpture 1648-1793, tome III (1689-1704), Paris: J. Baur, 1880, p. 268, assembly of 6 July 1699: a 'Discours sur la necessite ... d'establir des principes certains a la Peinture et a la Sculpture'. Scan: archive.org procsverbauxde03acaduoft

Same volume, p. 268 (6 July 1699): the Protector 'a fort recommande a la Compagnie d'en faire le cas qu'il merite' and said the Academie should address him through De Piles. Earlier, p. 259 (25 April 1699): the Compagnie invites him to take a seat among the Conseillers honoraires. The Discours itself is not transcribed in the volume.

De Piles, Cours de peinture par principes, Paris: Jacques Estienne, 1708, 'La Balance des Peintres', pp. 489-490: 'J'ay fait cet essai plutot pour me divertir que pour attirer les autres dans mon sentiment'; made at the request of 'quelques personnes'; 20 degrees. Scan: archive.org bub_gb_NlS7XHJ_tuYC (OCR read; privilege 23 Jan 1708, approbation of the censor Raguet 19 Jan 1708 on the whole book: 'tres-utile et tres-agreable au Public')

J. Richardson, An Essay on the Theory of Painting, London: W. Bowyer for John Churchill, 1715, p. 230-231: the scale 'is Curious, and Useful' but 'gives not a just Idea of the Masters' (Rembrandt rated above Michelangelo). Two Discourses, London: W. Churchill, 1719, discourse I, p. 55 (folio read from OCR): 'with a little Alteration and Improvement may be of great use to Lovers of Art, and Connoisseurs', then pp. 55-56 his own revised scale. A single connoisseur adopting the scale with corrections, 6 years after De Piles's death (Procès-verbaux IV, p. 81 by inference from the next page header, assembly of 6 April 1709: died 'hier, cinquieme du present mois'). Scans: archive.org bim_eighteenth-century_an-essay-on-the-theory-o_richardson-jonathan_1715, twodiscoursesies00rich

Mairan, 'Remarques sur la Balance des Peintres de M. de Piles', Memoires de l'Academie royale des sciences, annee 1755 (Paris: Imprimerie royale, 1761), Memoires p. 1 ff.; summary in the Histoire, section Geometrie, p. 79: 'L'idee de M. de Piles est ingenieuse et nouvelle' but 'il n'en est pas de meme du cote de l'execution'; Mairan's main correction is that the four degrees should be multiplied, not added. Mairan adopts the idea as 'essais de justesse'. Scan: archive.org histoiredelacad55acad. This is the 'Mairan 1755' item the Perplexity spec attached to Richardson; it concerns De Piles.

Graddy, 'Taste Endures! The Rankings of Roger de Piles (d. 1709) and Three Centuries of Art Prices', Journal of Economic History 73(3), 2013, pp. 766-791, doi 10.1017/S0022050713000600 (abstract read via Crossref: his overall ratings 'have withstood the test of a very long period of time'); Ginsburgh and Weyers, 'De Piles, Drawing and Color. An Essay in Quantitative Art History', Artibus et Historiae 23(45), 2002, pp. 191-203 (citation verified via Crossref; text not read in full). Scholars treating the ratings as a usable instrument is recorded as a field-level grant; predictive power is NOT counted as proof he was right.

Richardson, Two Discourses, London: W. Churchill, 1719, discourse II title page: 'An Argument in behalf of the Science of a Connoisseur; wherein is shewn the Dignity, Certainty, Pleasure, and Advantage of it'; addressed to 'Gentlemen who are Not yet Lovers, and Connoisseurs' (discourse II p. 157). Scan: archive.org twodiscoursesies00rich

Traite de la peinture et de la sculpture, par Mrs. Richardson, pere et fils, Amsterdam: Herman Uytwerf, 1728, 3 vols; vol. II title page: 'Un Discours sur la Science d'un Connoisseur ... Traduit de l'Anglois, revu et corrige par l'Auteur' (nine years after 1719; Richardson d. 1745). A translation exists and the author revised it; no sales or review evidence was found. Scans: archive.org bub_gb_54yu83dWracC, bub_gb_CMR_s1fWdKkC

James Northcote, Memoirs of Sir Joshua Reynolds, London: Henry Colburn, 1813, p. 179: of Richardson's 'Science of a Connoisseur' 'The whole subject is well handled by Richardson, and may be read with pleasure'. One painter-biographer, 68 years after Richardson's death. (Not coded: Northcote pp. 10-11 say Reynolds as a boy read Richardson's Theory of Painting and had his 'first fondness for his art excited' by it; that is reception of the Theory, undated, not of the connoisseurship claim.) Scan: archive.org memoirsofsirjosh01nort
fr.wikipedia 'Salons (Diderot)' (secondary, read): nine Salons written 1759-1781 for Grimm's Correspondance litteraire. Primary text not read.

ARTFL (Univ. of Chicago) 'Grimm's Correspondance litteraire' page (read): newsletter 'distributed between 1753 and 1790', a 'very small' subscriber base including European nobles; Diderot 'first published' the Salons there. fr.wikipedia 'Salons (Diderot)': each copy handwritten for a subscriber. Subscriber count not found.

fr.wikipedia 'Salons (Diderot)' (secondary, read): Salons de 1765 et 1767 edited posthumously by J.-A. Naigeon, Paris, 1800, vol. 13 (cites Gallica; not opened). One editor printing the text. Another snippet gave 1795 for the first printing; the dates conflict and are unresolved.
perplexity-2026-11-14: 'fame among later writers'. No source found for canon status or for the date. Kept as low confidence; excluded from the evidence-grade pass.

field_changes.change: numbered scales become an instrument scholars use to test reputation against later prices and acclaim (Graddy 2013)
the Salons, written for a handful of manuscript subscribers, are printed for a general readership (Naigeon, 1800, per fr.wikipedia)
